items.title: Count Minnesota MFIP RSDI only above the federal SSI maximum (Minn. Stat. 256P.06, subd. 3(2)(xvi))
items.body:
## Problem

Minnesota MFIP counts the full Social Security (RSDI) payment as unearned income. Since September 1, 2024, Minn. Stat. 256P.06, subd. 3(2)(xvi) counts, for chapter 142G (MFIP) and chapter 142E (CCAP), only the RSDI amount above the federal maximum SSI payment.

- **Current code.** `policyengine_us/parameters/gov/states/mn/dcyf/mfip/income/sources/unearned.yaml` lists `social_security` with no offset.
- **CCAP.** PolicyEngine/policyengine-us#10333 applies the rule to CCAP only, through the person-level `mn_ccap_countable_rsdi`.

## Law

**Minn. Stat. 256P.06, subd. 3(2)(xvi)** ([2025 text](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/256P.06)):

> for the purposes of programs under chapters 142E and 142G, the amount of retirement, survivors, and disability insurance payments that exceeds the applicable monthly federal maximum Supplemental Security Income payments.

- **History.** Laws 2023, ch. 70, art. 10, s. 79 added the item, naming chapters 119B and 256J. It is effective September 1, 2024. Item (viii) now counts full RSDI only for chapters 256D and 256I.
- **Agency guidance.** [Combined Manual 0017.15.45](https://www.dhs.state.mn.us/main/idcplg?IdcService=GET_DYNAMIC_CONVERSION&RevisionSelectionMethod=LatestReleased&dDocName=cm_00171545) (issue date 11/2024), MFIP and DWP: "For each client who receives RSDI, count only the gross RSDI amount that exceeds the SSI standard amount for a household of 1 as unearned income." Its 09/2024 revision note says the change "applies to MFIP, DWP, and CCAP."
- **Rate.** The monthly individual SSI federal benefit rate is in `gov.ssa.ssi.amount.individual` ($967 in 2025, $994 in 2026).

## Example (2026)

`policyengine_us/tests/policy/baseline/gov/states/mn/dcyf/mfip/mn_mfip_gross_unearned_income.yaml` Case 2 has $3,600 a year of `social_security` ($300 a month), $1,200 of child support and $600 of financial assistance.

- **Now:** 300 + 100 + 50 = **$450** a month.
- **Under (xvi):** max(300 − 994, 0) = 0, so 0 + 100 + 50 = **$150** a month.
- The federal `tanf_gross_unearned_income` (450 in that case) is a separate baseline and does not change.

## Suggested fix

1. Move the per-person offset into a program-neutral variable for the 256P.06 rule, so that CCAP and MFIP share one formula. For example, rename `mn_ccap_countable_rsdi` after #10333 merges.
2. Put that variable in place of `social_security` in the MFIP unearned list.
3. Keep the start date: the MFIP list starts in 2010, so the offset needs a parameter or start date for September 1, 2024. Before that date, MFIP counted gross RSDI.
4. Update the MFIP expectations that include RSDI, with hand-computed values, and add a case on each side of the 2024-09-01 start date.
5. Check `policyengine_us/tests/policy/baseline/partners/**` for MFIP households with Social Security. Edits there need Ziming Hua's approval under CLAUDE.md.

## Axiom

TheAxiomFoundation/rulespec-us#1869 asks for item (xvi) for both chapter 142E and chapter 142G, so the MFIP PR can cite it.

items.title: Disconnected disability inputs: repo-wide audit of disability gates vs their legal definitions
items.body:
## Summary

#9329 found that the Medicaid community-engagement exemption and the SSI disability pathway run on two disconnected inputs. A repo-wide sweep (2026-08-24; ~160 files across six program families; every confirmed finding checked against fetched statutory or manual text) shows this is a systemic class, not a one-off: **38 confirmed and 7 suspected** wiring defects where a program's legal disability test doesn't match the input the formula reads.

This umbrella documents the input taxonomy and fix patterns, tracks the high-priority findings filed as child issues, and holds the long tail as a checklist.

## The disconnected inputs

These person-level flags never imply each other — a person flagged on one side is invisible to every program wired to the other side:

| Variable | What it is |
|---|---|
| `is_disabled` | formula-less input; broad, undefined severity |
| `is_blind` | formula-less input; shared by both sides (why blind cases often escape the bug) |
| `meets_ssi_disability_criteria` | formula-less input; SSI §1614 medical criteria before the SGA screen |
| `is_ssi_disabled` | `meets_ssi_disability_criteria & ~ssi_engaged_in_sga` — the full 42 USC 1382c(a)(3) definition |
| `is_ssi_aged_blind_disabled` | aged \| blind \| SSI-disabled — does **not** include generic `is_disabled` |
| `is_permanently_and_totally_disabled` | formula-less input; the IRC §22(e)(3)-style P&T standard |
| `is_incapable_of_self_care` | formula-less input; the IRC §21 CDCC standard |
| `social_security_disability` | SSDI dollars; `> 0` is the SSDI-receipt proxy |
| `ssi` / `uncapped_ssi` | actual receipt (incl. income test + takeup) / passes the federal income test |

## Defect directions

- **A** — law cross-references the SSI/SSA definition or benefit receipt; code reads only generic `is_disabled` (the #9329 pattern)
- **B** — law has a narrower or different standard; the generic flag over-includes (or a covered group, e.g. the blind, is dropped)
- **C** — receipt-vs-definition mismatch
- **D** — sibling provisions wired differently with no legal basis

## Fix shapes (all additive or flag swaps — nothing needs generic `is_disabled` removed where the law is genuinely broad)

1. **OR in SSI-side flags** (`meets_ssi_disability_criteria` / `is_ssi_disabled`) where the law cross-references §1614 or SSA criteria
2. **Use receipt** (`ssi > 0`, `social_security_disability > 0`, `total_disability_payments`) where the law says "receives"
3. **Swap to `is_permanently_and_totally_disabled`** for "totally and permanently disabled" (§22-style) statutes
4. **Use `is_incapable_of_self_care`** for IRC §21-derived provisions

## High-priority findings (child issues)

- [ ] #9331 — SNAP unfitness exemptions (ABAWD, work registration, student rule)
- [ ] #9332 — `is_usda_disabled` receipt semantics + dropped blind SSI recipients
- [ ] #9333 — SSI student earned income exclusion
- [ ] #9334 — Medicaid home equity family exception
- [ ] #9335 — AR Medicaid work requirement (state analogue of #9329)
- [ ] #9336 — CA WDP and IL HBWD working-disabled buy-ins
- [ ] #9337 — HUD person-with-disabilities definition
- [ ] #9338 — CO AND-CS state supplement receipt gate
- [ ] #9339 — MA EAEDC SSI-eligibility exclusion (missing income test)
- [ ] #9340 — TANF classification gates (MT two-parent, VA TANF-UP, DC resource limit)
- [ ] #9329 — federal Medicaid work requirement (the original finding; still unfixed)

## Remaining confirmed findings (tracked here)

### State tax provisions

| Provision | File | Law | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| DE elderly/disabled exclusion | `de_elderly_or_disabled_income_exclusion_eligible_person.py:22` | [30 Del. C. §1106(b)(3)](https://delcode.delaware.gov/title30/c011/sc02/index.html): "total and permanent disability" | `is_permanently_and_totally_disabled` |
| GA retirement exclusion | `ga_retirement_exclusion_eligible_person.py:22` | [O.C.G.A. §48-7-27(a)(5)](https://codes.findlaw.com/ga/title-48-revenue-and-taxation/ga-code-sect-48-7-27/): permanent, "incapable of performing any gainful occupation" | `is_permanently_and_totally_disabled` |
| ID aged/disabled credit + deduction | `id_aged_or_disabled_credit_eligible_person.py:18`, `id_aged_or_disabled_deduction_eligible_person.py:18` | [Idaho Code §63-3025D](https://legislature.idaho.gov/statutesrules/idstat/title63/t63ch30/sect63-3025d/): **developmental disability** per §66-402 only | needs a new developmental-disability input (see below) |
| ID retirement benefits deduction | `id_retirement_benefits_eligible_person.py:16` | §63-3022A → [§63-701](https://legislature.idaho.gov/statutesrules/idstat/title63/t63ch7/sect63-701/): "recognized as disabled by the social security administration" or other listed agency | P&T flag or receipt disjunction |
| HI disabled exemption | `hi_disabled_exemptions.py:19` | HRS §235-54(c) / [Haw. Admin. R. §18-235-1.11](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/hawaii/Haw-Code-R-SS-18-235-1-11): "blind, deaf, or totally disabled" — **blind never read** | `is_permanently_and_totally_disabled \| is_blind`; deaf unmodeled |
| MD pension subtraction | `md_pension_subtraction_amount.py:21` | [Tax-Gen §10-209](https://law.justia.com/codes/maryland/tax-general/title-10/subtitle-2/part-ii/section-10-209/): "totally disabled", physician-certified | P&T flag for person and spouse |
| NJ pension exclusion | `nj_eligible_pension_income.py:20` | [NJ Div. of Taxation](https://www.nj.gov/treasury/taxation/njit7.shtml): "disabled as defined by Social Security guidelines" | `is_permanently_and_totally_disabled \| is_blind` |
| OR WFHDC credit | `or_wfhdc_has_qualified_individual_eligible.py:23`, `or_wfhdc_eligibility_category.py:36` | [ORS 315.264](https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_315.264) keys to IRC §21; federal CDCC in-repo already reads the right flag | `is_incapable_of_self_care` |

Code §27-33-67(2)](https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-27/chapter-33/article-1/section-27-33-67/): totally disabled under the Social Security Act (42 USC 416(i)), RRA, or other federal act | P&T flag or receipt gate |

| MN M1PR + renters credit | `mn_homestead_credit_refund_household_income.py:78`, `mn_renters_credit_household_income.py:29` | [M1PR instructions](https://www.taxformfinder.org/forms/2024/2024-minnesota-form-m1pr-instructions.pdf#page=9): SSA-certified, 12-month unable-to-work, **or blind** — blind claimants lose the $5,050 subtraction | add `\| is_blind` in both |
| MT disabled-dependent exemption | `mt_dependent_exemptions_person.py:20` | [ARM 42.15.403](https://regulations.justia.com/states/montana/department-42/chapter-42-15/subchapter-42-15-4/rule-42-15-403/): physician-certified permanent disability ≥ 50% of body (historical years; repealed 2024) | P&T flag; low priority |

### Other confirmed

- [ ] `disabled_head`/`disabled_spouse` (household/demographic/tax_unit) read `is_ssi_disabled` while siblings `head_is_disabled`/`spouse_is_disabled` read generic `is_disabled`; consumers are NJ (N.J.S.A. 54A:3-1(b) — §22-style definition, no SSI reference) and NH RSA 77:5. Direction D — rewire to generic `is_disabled` and consider consolidating the duplicate pairs.
- [ ] IL HBWD worker test (`il_hbwd_countable_earned_income.py:24`) narrower than its own eligibility test — an SSDI-receipt-only worker passes eligibility but is denied the §120.510(i) earned-income exemptions. Fix: derive from `il_hbwd_disability_eligible`. (Grouped with the buy-in child issue.)
- [ ] CalWORKs resource limit (`ca_tanf_resources_limit.py:19`): [CalWORKs 42-200](https://my.dpss.lacounty.gov/public/en/home/epolicy/program/calworks/property/property.html) / [ACL 22-66](https://cdss.ca.gov/Portals/9/Additional-Resources/Letters-and-Notices/ACLs/2022/22-66.pdf#page=2) require impairment **and** receipt (SDI, Workers' Comp TD, IHSS, SSI/SSP) for adults. Fix: receipt-based adult leg; keep broad flag for children (their definition is genuinely broad).
- [ ] DC POWER (`dc_power_head_or_spouse_eligible.py:24`): [DC Code §4-205.72](https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/4-205.72) is a cannot-work standard, not self-care. Fix: use `is_disabled` (or OR both) for the incapacity leg.
- [ ] Denver property tax relief (`has_co_denver_dhs_elderly_disabled.py:14`): [Denver program](https://denvergov.org/Government/Agencies-Departments-Offices/Agencies-Departments-Offices-Directory/Department-of-Housing-Stability/Resident-Resources/Property-Tax-Relief) requires SGA-inability **and** receipt of a public benefit payment. Fix: at minimum OR SSI/SSDI receipt; document unmodeled CO/Denver payment legs.
- [ ] MS CCPP special-needs child (`ms_ccpp_eligible_child.py:15`, `ms_ccpp_maximum_weekly_rate.py:40`, `ms_ccpp_minimum_fee_category.py:25`): the [CCPP manual](https://www.mdhs.ms.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/CCPP-Policy-Manual_Final_1142025.pdf#page=10) defines "child with special needs" verbatim as the SSI child disability standard (42 USC 1382c(a)(3)(C)(i)), with IEP/IFSP as the alternate verification channel. Fix: `meets_ssi_disability_criteria | has_individualized_education_program` in all three gates.

## Suspected findings (needs verification before filing fixes)

- [ ] **MS Healthier Mississippi Waiver** (`ms_hmw_demographic_eligible.py:17`) ignores SSDI receipt — an SSDI recipient in the 24-month Medicare waiting period is the target population but is missed; MS's own `ms_wd_disability_eligible` accepts `ssdi > 0`. The [waiver STCs](https://medicaid.ms.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Healthier-Mississippi-Extension.pdf#page=8) don't define "disabled" — verify against MS ABD policy (Chapter 400).
- [ ] **IN RCAP** (`in_ssp_rcap_eligible.py:20`) requires `is_ssi_aged_blind_disabled`, but IC 12-10-6-2.1(a)'s condition is functional (dementia/mental illness/physical disability), not SSI's ABD categories — Medicaid recipients under 65 with dementia/mental illness are missed.
- [ ] **MT TANF blanket exemption** (`mt_tanf_meets_work_requirements.py:18`): per TANF 705-1 incapacity only re-classifies hours; only SSI recipients are excluded from work-eligible individuals. Verify whether a broader WoRC exemption list exists elsewhere in the DPHHS manual.
- [ ] **MN MFIP adult-care deduction** (`mn_mfip_dependent_care_deduction.py:23`): [MN Stat. 142G.16](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/142G.16) covers children only; the adult leg rests on Combined Manual 0018.09 (bot-walled, unfetchable). ME's identical concept uses `is_incapable_of_self_care`; MN uses `is_disabled` — one is presumably mis-keyed.
- [ ] **MS CCPP activity waiver** (`ms_ccpp_activity_eligible.py:23`): the manual pairs the SSI definition with "current documentation of SSI benefits"; ambiguous whether that conditions eligibility or only priority ranking. If eligibility: `is_ssi_disabled & ((ssi > 0) | receives_ssi)`.
- [ ] **OK CCS predetermined eligibility** (`ok_ccs_predetermined_eligible.py:23`): checks only computed `ssi > 0`; siblings MD/MI/MO/LA all use `(ssi > 0) | receives_ssi`. Minor repo-consistency fix.
- [ ] **DC disabled exclusion subtraction** (`dc_disabled_exclusion_subtraction.py:21`): receipt list omits railroad/federal/DC disability benefits that the D-40 rule lists and the property-tax sibling captures via `total_disability_payments`.

## Not representable today (documented non-modeling, not defects)

- **Developmental disability**: Idaho §63-3025D/§63-3022E and Arkansas §26-51-503 cover *only* developmental disabilities. No existing input fits — either add a `has_developmental_disability`-type input or record an explicit not-modeled decision. Generic `is_disabled` is the worst available choice for both.
- **7 CFR 271.2 remainder**: government disability retirement (SSA §221(i)-permanent) and Railroad Retirement disability annuities have no model inputs (`railroad_benefits` has no disability split).

## Notes

- Three files (KY, WA, IN property tax) carry comments admitting the generic flag is a proxy — the repo has known about this class locally but has no policy. This issue is intended to be that policy reference.
- Microsimulation impact depends on which flags the dataset actually populates (e.g. whether `meets_ssi_disability_criteria` is imputed for non-recipients). Direction-A bugs bite in microsim only where SSI-side flags are set; all of them bite in household calculations and the API.

items.title: Implement New Hampshire LIHEAP regular heating assistance
items.body:
## Summary

Implement New Hampshire's LIHEAP regular heating benefit, the Fuel Assistance Program (FAP), for program year 2027 (the 2026-2027 heating season). The New Hampshire Department of Energy runs the program through community action agencies under the PY2027 Fuel Assistance Program Policy and Procedures Manual.

## Scope

Regular heating assistance only, as part of the all-state LIHEAP effort: household composition, countable income, the income limit, the housing and heating-cost conditions, the annual heating cost (actual bill or the manual's heating cost formula) and the benefit matrix. Crisis and emergency assistance, cooling, weatherization, heating-equipment repair, the supplemental benefit and Senior Energy Assistance Services are out of scope.

## Key rules

- Income limit: 60% of state median income for the household size, inclusive (manual pages 17 and 74; plan section 2.1). The PY2027 limits run from $48,713 for one person to $129,278 for eight. Federal law bars excluding a household on income alone when its income is below 110% of the poverty guideline (42 U.S.C. 8624(b)(2)(B)).
- Household size counts U.S. citizens and qualified noncitizens; ineligible members' income still counts (manual pages 12 and 34 to 36). No asset test and no categorical eligibility (plan section 2.3; manual page 12).
- Countable income: gross wages, net self-employment and rental income, Social Security, SSI for adults, pensions including military retirement pay, railroad retirement, unemployment, workers' compensation, veterans payments, state welfare including FANF, alimony, taxable gambling winnings, and interest and dividends over $50 a year. Child support received, capital gains, SSI for children under 18 and the earnings of full-time high school students are excluded. Child support paid and Medicare Part B and Part D premiums are deducted (manual pages 15 to 17). Page 16 excludes the first $50 of interest and the first $50 of dividends separately, while page 17 allows "$50 of earned interest and/or dividends annually."
- Housing: subsidized tenants whose heat is included in rent are ineligible; subsidized tenants who pay their own heating bill qualify (manual page 21). Unsubsidized tenants with heat in rent qualify, and the plan says their benefits are reduced without stating the reduction (plan section 2.3).
- Annual heating cost: the actual annual cost or the estimate dwelling factor x rooms x agency heating degree days / 1,000,000 x fuel cost per MBTU / fuel efficiency, whichever gives the better benefit (manual pages 17 to 18 and 76 to 77). Cost tiers are DD under $1,000, CC $1,000 to $1,749.99, BB $1,750 to $3,499.99 and AA $3,500 or more.
- Payment: the Attachment D matrix (manual page 78) by cost tier and income level, A at or below 75% of the poverty guideline through E at or below 175% and F above 175% up to the income limit. Deliverable fuels receive $400 to $2,500; electricity and natural gas receive 75% of the deliverable amount.

## Sources

- PY2027 Fuel Assistance Program Policy and Procedures Manual (program schedule page 10; eligibility pages 12 and 21; income pages 15 to 17; household members pages 34 to 36; income guidelines, heating cost formula and benefit matrix in Attachments B to D, pages 74 to 78): https://www.energy.nh.gov/sites/g/files/ehbemt551/files/inline-documents/sonh/fuel-assistance-program-procedures-manual.pdf#page=10
- FY2026 LIHEAP state plan (sections 2.1 and 2.3, page 8): https://liheapch.acf.gov/docs/2026/state-plans/NH_Plan_2026.pdf#page=8
- FFY2027 LIHEAP Detailed Model Plan draft (section 2.3, page 8): https://www.energy.nh.gov/sites/g/files/ehbemt551/files/inline-documents/low-income-home-energy-assistance-detailed-model-plan.pdf#page=8
- 42 U.S.C. 8624(b)(2)(B): https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/8624#b_2_B
- Community Action Partnership of New Hampshire agency county service areas: https://www.capnh.org/home-old

## Related

- #256 (LIHEAP epic) and #9754 (`heating_type` default).

items.title: Investigate USDA/SNAP disabled status modeling and data support
items.body:
## Context

While making `meets_ssi_disability_criteria` input-only, we noticed that SNAP fixtures should not use SSI disability criteria as a proxy for SNAP elderly/disabled status. SNAP has a separate `is_usda_disabled` concept, and USDA/SNAP disability rules are not the same as SSI disability criteria.

Current PE-US structure is directionally right: `has_usda_elderly_disabled` uses `is_usda_disabled`, and `is_usda_disabled` is driven by `gov.usda.disabled_programs`, currently including `is_ssi_disabled`, `social_security_disability`, permanent disabled veteran, and surviving spouse/child of disabled veteran. But the statutory definition in 7 U.S.C. § 2012(j) appears broader and program/status-based, not a general functional limitation or raw SSI medical-criteria screen.

## Why this matters

SNAP special rules for elderly/disabled households affect the gross income test, asset test, excess shelter deduction cap, medical expense deduction, and work/student rules. We should avoid using `meets_ssi_disability_criteria` or generic `is_disabled` as a shortcut for SNAP disability status unless the law supports that specific path.

## Things to investigate

- Compare PE-US `is_usda_disabled` against the full 7 U.S.C. § 2012(j) elderly/disabled member definition and FNS guidance.
- Identify which statutory qualifying statuses are currently missing from PE-US, e.g. state disability-based assistance, qualifying Medicaid/disability-related medical assistance, government disability retirement, Railroad Retirement disability annuity, and the full VA/survivor categories.
- Decide whether PE-US needs additional input variables or formulas for missing USDA qualifying statuses.
- In policyengine-us-data, check whether CPS/SIPP contain source variables for any missing USDA qualifying statuses.
- If source variables are missing, decide whether they should be imputed separately from SSI disability criteria, or left unmodeled with documentation.
- Ensure SNAP tests/fixtures use `is_usda_disabled` or qualifying program/status inputs directly, not `meets_ssi_disability_criteria`.

## References

- 7 U.S.C. § 2012(j): https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/7/2012
- FNS SNAP special rules for elderly/disabled households: https://www.fns.usda.gov/snap/eligibility/elderly-disabled-special-rules

items.title: Implement Washington LIHEAP regular heating assistance
items.body:
## Summary

Implement Washington's LIHEAP regular heating benefit for FY2026. The Washington State Department of Commerce runs the program through local agencies under the FFY2026 state plan. Agencies compute the regular benefit with the Commerce Actual and Surrogate Heat Cost benefit calculation worksheet.

## Scope

Regular heating assistance only, as part of the all-state LIHEAP effort: income eligibility, household composition, countable income, heating responsibility, and the worksheet benefit with its minimum and maximum. Crisis assistance, cooling, weatherization, heating-equipment repair and the $20.01 SNAP nominal payment are out of scope.

## Key rules

- Income limit: 150% of the HHS poverty guideline, with no asset test and no categorical eligibility (plan sections 1.4, 2.1 and 2.3). FY2026 uses the 2025 guideline; the PY27 eligibility sheet uses the 2026 guideline.
- Household: recipients must be U.S. citizens or qualified noncitizens (plan section 17.3). The plan does not state how mixed-status households are counted.
- Countable income: the plan selects gross income (section 1.8) and checks wages, self-employment, unemployment, strike pay, Social Security, SSI, retirement and pension benefits, general assistance, TANF, repayable loans, cash gifts, jury duty pay, rental income, work-study income, alimony, child support, interest, dividends and royalties, commissions, structured legal settlements and foster care payments (section 1.9). VA benefits, insurance payments, one-time lump sums, tax refunds and earnings of children under 18 are not counted. Commerce Policy 1.1.2 applies a 20% allowance to wages and 10% deductions to retirement and unemployment income at the 150% threshold, and the Byrd Barr Place application takes the 20% deduction on earned income taxed at payout. Agencies count self-employment net of allowable expenses, with a loss month counted as zero, and deduct child support paid.
- Heating responsibility: the household pays a heating bill or has heat included in rent (Byrd Barr Place application).
- Benefit (worksheet): monthly income divided by a household-size adjuster (1.00 for one person up to 9.21 for 24 people) is subtracted from 3,648.10. Dividing 1,460.80 by that result and subtracting the quotient from 1.30 gives the heat cost multiplier, which multiplies the annual heat cost. The plan sets a $250 minimum and a $1,250 maximum (section 2.6).

## Sources

- FFY2026 LIHEAP state plan (sections 1.4, 1.8, 1.9, 2.1, 2.3, 2.6 and 17.3; pages 5 to 10 and 37): https://liheapch.acf.gov/docs/2026/state-plans/WA_Plan_2026.pdf#page=5

## Summary

Implement Louisiana's LIHEAP regular heating benefit for FY2026 (October 1, 2025 to September 30, 2026). The Louisiana Housing Corporation (LHC) pays one heating-season award from the FFY2026 Heating and Cooling Benefit Matrix, set by the household's energy burden and size, plus a $100 supplement for priority households. The Louisiana LIHEAP Service Delivery Guide revised January 1, 2024 governed the FY2026 heating season; the edition effective April 1, 2026 keeps the same income, burden and benefit rules.

## Scope

Regular heating assistance only, as part of the all-state LIHEAP effort: household size, countable income, the 60% state median income limit, responsibility for energy costs, total energy cost and the subsidized-housing utility allowance, the matrix award, the zero-income rule and the priority supplement. The summer cooling cycle (the same matrix used in the cooling season), crisis assistance, weatherization, equipment repair or replacement and discretionary supplemental heating payments are out of scope.

## Key rules

- Income limit: 60% of state median income for all household sizes (FY2026 plan 2.1; guide 3.6 C.1). Notice LHP-2025-01 prints annual limits from $30,618 for one person to $84,790 for ten. Income may not exceed the limit. The federal floor in 42 U.S.C. 8624(b)(2)(B) protects income below 110% of the poverty guideline; in FY2026 it exceeds the 60% limit from household size 14.
- Household: the applicant must be a citizen or a permanent legal resident eligible for federal benefits, and a household of only ineligible aliens does not qualify. Undocumented members are left out of household size, but their income counts (guide 3.6 D and D.3). The April 2026 edition adds a household-member definition with exclusions, such as children away at school.
- Heating cost and responsibility: the applicant must be fully or partly responsible for a residential energy bill. Renters whose heat is in the rent qualify; the landlord states the monthly heating cost on Appendix L and passes the benefit on as a rent reduction (guide 3.6 E; plan 2.3).
- Countable income: gross income of every member 18 or older, including undocumented members (guide 3.6 C.1 and Appendix E). Counted: wages, net self-employment, Social Security net of the Medicare deduction (plan 1.9), SSI, pensions, railroad retirement, veterans' payments, unemployment, workers' compensation, strike benefits, alimony, interest, dividends, net rental income, estate and trust receipts, net gambling winnings, regular contributions and FITAP. Not counted: child support, capital gains, bank and retirement-account withdrawals, tax refunds, irregular gifts, one-time payments and SNAP, nor the earnings of members under 18 or of members 18 and over still in high school. Social Security and SSI paid to minors count (Appendix E; FAQ A4).
- Benefit computation: energy burden is the monthly total energy cost, the sum of every energy vendor's bill not more than 30 days old, divided by monthly income (guide 4.1 and 4.2). The FFY2026 matrix pays $200, $350, $500 or $650 for one to three members and $250, $400, $550 or $700 for four or more, for burdens of 9.9% and less, 10% to 17.9%, 18% to 24.9% and 25% and greater. Households with zero income receive the maximum for their size. One $100 supplement per household with a member 60 or older, disabled, or five or younger (guide 4.2 A). The plan's range is $200 to $800 (plan 2.6); there is no bill cap.
- Special housing: subsidized households subtract their utility allowance from the total energy cost; an allowance greater than the bill makes the household ineligible, and applicants 60 or older are exempt (guide 4.1 C; plan 2.3). The April 2026 edition compares the allowance with the bill for the same utility. Community solar participants use the same calculation (plan 2.5).

items.body:
## Summary

Implement Wisconsin's Home Energy Assistance Program (WHEAP) regular heating benefit, the federal LIHEAP heat benefit, for FFY2026 (October 1, 2025 to September 30, 2026). The Department of Administration's Division of Energy, Housing and Community Resources runs the program under Wis. Stat. 16.27 and the Program Year 2026 WHEAP Manual. The benefit formula and heat proxy table come from the FFY2026 Home Energy Plus (HE+) Benefit Calculator, Wisconsin's benefit matrix on the LIHEAP Clearinghouse.

## Scope

Regular heating assistance only, as part of the all-state LIHEAP effort. Out of scope: the state-funded non-heating electric (Public Benefits) benefit, crisis assistance, weatherization, HE+ Program Services, supplemental benefits, the February 1 payment reduction and the $1 SNAP benefit of Wis. Stat. 16.27(5)(e).

## Key rules

- Income limit: gross income at or below 60% of state median income (Wis. Stat. 16.27(5)(b); manual 3.3.1). PY26 limits run from $38,421 for one person to $128,565 for twenty (manual Appendix E; calculator SMI_Lookup), on one month of income, annualized. A household in which every member receives W-2 cash, FoodShare or SSI for the prior month passes the income test (16.27(5)(c); manual 3.3.1 item 2) and is paid as if its income equaled the limit (manual 2.3.1 item 1). 42 U.S.C. 8624(b)(2)(B) bars excluding a household with income below 110% of the poverty guideline.
- Household: the economic unit living together on the application date (16.27(1)(c); manual 3.2.6), less temporary members, students living away and court-placed foster children (3.2.6.4). Citizens and eligible non-citizens, including non-citizens who receive FoodShare or monthly Social Security, count in household size; ineligible non-citizens' income counts but they do not (manual 3.2.2.4 and 4.4.26.2). The case head must be a citizen or eligible non-citizen (3.2.1).
- Heating cost and responsibility: the household needs an energy burden: a heating bill it pays, heat in rent, or payments to the landlord (manual 3.2.5). It reports one primary fuel; kerosene, pellets and other biofuels are "wood or other" (4.4.28.2 and 4.4.28.3).
- Countable income: gross income of all members in the prior month (manual 3.3.2). Earned income of members under 18 and of high school students is ignored. Self-employment, farm and rental income are netted across sources and members, a net loss counting as zero (3.3.5). Social Security and Railroad Retirement count less Medicare premiums (Table 3.5); SSI, pensions, withdrawals at 73 or older, veterans benefits, workers' compensation, disability, alimony, child support, interest and dividends of $120 or more, gambling, gifts and W-2 cash count (Table 3.4); court-ordered child support paid is deducted. Unemployment compensation and most lump sums are ignored (Table 3.6). No asset test.
- Benefit computation (calculator Computation and HT_Proxy sheets; manual 2.3.1): benefit = (2.66667 - poverty ratio) / 2.94269 x heating cost, where the ratio of income to the 2025 poverty guideline is held between 0.60 and 2.15. The heating cost is the reported bill, less 60% for electric heat, held between 0.75 and 2 times a heat proxy; the proxy is a base plus a per-room amount times rooms (1 to 9), by fuel class (five) and dwelling type (five). Amounts are truncated and not paid below $30. The maximum is $2,147 (ACF plan), $2,580 (agency plan) or $2,575 (calculator); the formula never exceeds $2,574.
- Special housing: heat included in rent is paid on 0.75 times the proxy. Rental assistance or public housing with heat in rent gives no energy burden; Section 42 (LIHTC) tenants keep it (manual 3.2.5.1, Table 3.2, 4.4.28.4). Subsidized tenants who pay their heating vendor are eligible (Wis. Stat. 16.27(5)(d)).

## Summary

Implement Minnesota's Energy Assistance Program (EAP) Primary Heat benefit, the state's single regular LIHEAP heating benefit, for FFY2026 and FFY2027. The Minnesota Department of Commerce runs EAP under the EAP Policy Manual (FFY26 and FFY27 editions, for the program years starting October 1, 2025 and October 1, 2026) and its Appendix 4A, the Primary Heat Benefit Calculator, which publishes the pay-share constants and the backup matrix. Primary Heat pays a share of the household's total annual home energy cost, including non-heat electricity.

## Scope

Regular heating assistance only, as part of the all-state LIHEAP effort: household size, countable income, the one-month income maximum, vulnerability to energy costs, the annual energy cost, the pay share, rounding, and the $200 minimum and $1,400 maximum. Crisis, Energy Related Repair, weatherization, Assurance 16 services, the application deadline, the one-grant-per-year rule and eHEAT's consumption-validation rules are out of scope.

## Key rules

- Income limit: one month of gross income at or below the one-month maximum, which is 50% of state median income for sizes 1 to 18 and 110% of the prior year's poverty guideline for sizes 19 and 20 (manual FFY26 pages 88-89, FFY27 page 90; plan 2.1). The FFY26 maximums run from $3,119 for one person to $11,013 for twenty; FFY27 from $3,205 to $11,355. Above size 20 the 110% floor of 42 U.S.C. 8624(b)(2)(B) applies.
- Household: individuals who live together as one economic unit buying energy in common or paying for it in rent (42 U.S.C. 8622(5); manual page 82). Ineligible non-citizens are left out of household size, but their income counts (pages 80-81; plan page 9).
- Heating cost and vulnerability: the household must pay an energy vendor or pay for heat in its rent. Households in Section 8, public or tribal subsidized housing with heat in rent qualify only if they pay electric costs, and those with heat and electricity included are ineligible (pages 72 and 126; plan 2.3).
- Countable income: one month of gross cash receipts of all members, including SSI, General Assistance, MFIP, unemployment and Minnesota Paid Leave. Social Security and PERA pensions count net of Medicare deductions; a self-employment loss on one return does not offset another; retirement withdrawals count from age 59½; dividends and interest count at $50 a month or more, and cash gifts at $100 or more. Child support, capital gains, Minnesota Supplemental Aid and foster care do not count, nor do the earnings and unemployment of K-12 students aged 19 or under (pages 88-102 and 107-111; FFY27 pages 96 and 116).
- Benefit computation: the income percentile is income divided by the maximum for the household size. The pay share falls linearly from 43.9% at percentile 0 to 10.8% at 0.896 in FFY26, and from 45.2% to 11.3% at 0.891 in FFY27 (Appendix 4A Formula Parameters). The benefit is the pay share times the annual energy cost, rounded to whole dollars and held between $200 and $1,400 (page 124; plan 2.6). Households whose only income is DWP, General Assistance, MFIP or SSI are placed at the lowest income level (page 102).
- Special housing: with heat in unsubsidized rent, the backup matrix supplies the average annual energy cost for each of seven main fuels and eight housing types. With heat in subsidized rent, the electric bill sets the cost (pages 118-126). A new housing-type input selects the matrix column.

items.title: Atomic inputs: one fact, one input — eliminate arbitration between redundant input variables
items.body:
## The rule

**One fact, one input, at its natural entity.** Derived aggregates are formulas, never alternative inputs; the model never arbitrates between two inputs describing the same real-world fact. This extends #8162's "inputs are pure leaves" (no formulas/adds/guards on inputs) to *unique* leaves: redundancy between pure leaves is where silent double-counts, ignored inputs, and fallback bugs breed — #9004/#9142 (mortgage) being the type specimen: two input vocabularies for one fact required arbitration logic, and the arbitration itself was the bug.

"Natural entity" is the entity where the fact actually attaches — usually person for money amounts, but e.g. loan-level facts (balance, origination year) park at tax_unit for want of a loan entity. Atomic ≠ everything person-level.

## Inventory (verified on main, 2026-08-13)

| Case | Inputs in conflict | Arbitration site |
|---|---|---|
| **Mortgage interest** | person `home_mortgage_interest` vs tax-unit `first/second_home_mortgage_interest` | `mortgage_interest_structure.py` (`where(structured > 0, …)`) and again in `home_mortgage_interest_share` |
| **Heating expenses** | person `heating_expense_person` vs spm-unit `heating_cooling_expense` vs per-fuel spm-unit `pre_subsidy_electricity_expense`/`gas_expense`/`fuel_oil_expense` | per-program: `dc_liheap_payment.py`, `il_liheap_base_payment.py` (each arbitrates differently) |
| **Subset markers** | `military_retirement_pay` must *also* be included in `taxable_pension_income` by the user; no arbitration, just a convention — forget either side and results are silently wrong (documented in the VT Act 71 test comments) | none (that's the problem) |
| **`_reported` overrides** | `ssi_reported`+`use_reported_ssi`, `medicare_part_b_premiums_reported`, `spm_unit_net_income_reported`, two state subtraction `_reported`s | explicit toggles |

Proposed disposition: migrate the first two to single inputs; add a validation check for subset markers (subset ≤ total); **exempt the `_reported` class explicitly** — data-vs-simulation switches are a deliberate, named pattern, not redundancy.

## Mortgage migration (staged — single-shot removal is unsafe)

Load-bearing constraint, verified in policyengine-core: the dataset loader **silently skips** h5 columns whose variable no longer exists (`simulation.py`: `if variable_name not in self.tax_benefit_system.variables: continue`). Certified microcosm h5s carry the structured columns, so deleting the inputs today would silently zero mortgage interest for existing data. (Core-side warning proposed separately.)

Also verified in microcosm: the structured interest columns are *derived* in the build's `mortgage_conversion` stage by splitting the person-level `home_mortgage_interest` total — the model then sums them back. The split is pure round-trip redundancy even inside the data pipeline; only the balances/origination years (needed for the §163(h)(3)(F) two-vintage caps, and never person-attributable — loans are joint) carry independent information.

1. **Now (pe-us):** flip arbitration — person-level `home_mortgage_interest` is canonical; structured interest is a deprecated fallback used only when the person-level sum is zero. Structured interest inputs documented as deprecated pointing here. Microsim-neutral whenever the h5's person column and split sum agree (they come from the same stage total; microcosm to confirm per-record reconciliation on the current certified build — receipt requested in the companion issue).
2. **Microcosm:** stop exporting `first/second_home_mortgage_interest` (keep person interest + balances + origination years) in the next certified build.
3. **After the first certified release without the columns (pe-us):** delete the structured interest inputs and the fallback (`removed` fragment). The known first/second interest split has no model consumer — the deduction formula only ever uses the sum.

Known line-item to resolve at stage 3: the tax-unit total counts all members while `home_mortgage_interest_share` allocates only across head/spouse — pick one convention (head/spouse is the defensible line for a filers' deduction).

## LIHEAP follow-up (separate PR)

Pick one heating-expense vocabulary (person-level `heating_expense_person` is the atomic candidate), migrate DC/IL/MA formulas, deprecate the rest on the same staged pattern (they are also microdata-supplied).

Refs: #9004, #9142, #8162, populace/microcosm#511.

items.title: Wire military retirement pay and survivor benefits into federal pension income and AGI
items.body:
### Summary
`military_retirement_pay` and `military_retirement_pay_survivors` are currently isolated leaf variables that are not connected to `taxable_public_pension_income`, `taxable_pension_income`, `irs_gross_income`, or `market_income`. 

Because nearly all state individual income taxes use federal adjusted gross income (AGI) as their baseline, omitting military retirement income from federal gross income breaks both federal and state tax calculations across the country.

---

### 1. Federal Tax & Program Impact

* **Federal Income Tax is $0**: Under [26 U.S. Code § 61](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/61) and IRS Publication 525 / Publication 3, military retirement pay and Survivor Benefit Plan (SBP) annuity payments are fully taxable ordinary pension income. Currently, federal gross income (`irs_gross_income`) and federal AGI (`adjusted_gross_income`) calculate as $0 for a retiree with military retirement income, resulting in $0 federal tax liability.
* **Means-Tested Benefits**:
  * **SNAP**: [7 CFR § 273.9(b)(2)(ii)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/7/273.9#b_2) counts military pensions as unearned income. PolicyEngine's SNAP unearned income sources list `pension_income`, which relies on `taxable_pension_income` and thus omits military pay.
  * **SSI**: [20 CFR § 416.1121(a)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/20/416.1121) counts periodic pension payments. SSI countable unearned income omits military retirement pay.
  * **Medicaid & ACA PTC**: Base eligibility on MAGI, which derives from federal AGI. Military retirees appear artificially low-income, improperly receiving Medicaid eligibility or excessive premium tax credits.
* **Aggregates & SPM**: `market_income`, `spm_unit_market_income`, and `spm_unit_net_income` omit military retirement pay.

---

### 2. Cascading State Tax Anomalies

Because states derive state taxable income from federal AGI, omitting military pay from federal AGI causes severe distortions:

1. **The "Tax-Shelter" Double-Deduction in Exemption States**:
   * Over 20 states have enacted subtractions/deductions for military retirement pay from federal AGI (e.g., AZ, CO, CT, DE, GA, ID, IA, LA, MD, ME, MI, MN, NE, NM, OK, RI, SC, VA, VT, WV).
   * Because federal AGI does not contain military pay, taking the state subtraction deducts against **other unrelated income** (such as employment wages).
   * *Example*: A veteran in Arizona or Virginia with $50,000 of wages and $20,000 of military retirement pay has a federal AGI of $50,000 in PolicyEngine. The state subtracts $20,000, reducing state taxable income to $30,000 and inappropriately shielding $20,000 of wages from state income tax.
   * In **Utah**, the nonrefundable military retirement credit (`military_retirement_pay * rate`) wipes out state tax owed on other income.

2. **Erroneous Full Exemption in Non-Exempt States**:
   * **California (CA)** and **Washington D.C. (DC)** fully tax military retirement pay. Because federal AGI is $0, PolicyEngine calculates $0 state income tax for military retirees living in CA and DC.
   * In states with statutory caps (e.g., Virginia caps at $30k in 2024 / $40k in 2025; Maryland caps at $12.5k / $20k; New Mexico caps at $30k), amounts *above* the cap are supposed to remain taxable. In PolicyEngine, 100% of the excess remains untaxed.

3. **Senior Dead-Zones in Colorado & Georgia**:
   * **Colorado**: `co_military_retirement_subtraction` is restricted to filers aged `< 55`. Filers aged 55+ are directed to the general pension subtraction (C.R.S. § 39-22-104(4)(f)), but Colorado's general pension sources (`co/tax/income/subtractions/pension/income_sources.yaml`) omit `military_retirement_pay`.
   * **Georgia**: `ga_military_retirement_exclusion_person` applies under age 62. The senior retirement exclusion for age 62+ (`ga/tax/income/agi/exclusions/retirement/sources.yaml`) also omits `military_retirement_pay`.

4. **Inconsistent Survivor Benefit Handling**:
   * `military_retirement_pay_survivors` is only recognized in 4 states (NC, SC, MD, MN). All other states with military exemptions only reference `military_retirement_pay`, ignoring survivor benefits if entered into the designated survivor variable.

---

### 3. Sibling Public Pension Variables
The same architectural gap affects other public pension variables:
* `csrs_retirement_pay` (Civil Service Retirement System)
* `taxable_federal_pension_income`

Neither variable feeds into `taxable_public_pension_income`, `taxable_pension_income`, or `irs_gross_income`.

---

### 4. Proposed Solution

1. **Wire Components into Federal Pension Income**:
   Add `military_retirement_pay`, `military_retirement_pay_survivors`, `taxable_federal_pension_income`, and `csrs_retirement_pay` to `taxable_public_pension_income` (or `taxable_pension_income`):
   ```python
   class taxable_public_pension_income(Variable):
       ...
       adds = [
           "military_retirement_pay",
           "military_retirement_pay_survivors",
           "taxable_federal_pension_income",
           "csrs_retirement_pay",
       ]
   ```
   *(Ensure leaf vs. aggregate behavior allows microdata that specifies the parent to continue working).*

2. **Include in `pension_income` / `market_income`**:
   Ensure both military retirement pay and survivor benefits flow into `pension_income` so SNAP, SSI, Medicaid/ACA MAGI, and SPM measures capture countable unearned income.

3. **Harmonize State Subtractions**:
   * For states that uniformly exempt both retiree pay and survivor benefits (AZ, CT, GA, ID, ME, NE, NM, OK, VA, etc.), sum both:
     ```python
     tax_unit_non_dep_add(tax_unit, period, ["military_retirement_pay", "military_retirement_pay_survivors"])
     ```
   * Preserve the distinction between `military_retirement_pay` and `military_retirement_pay_survivors` for North Carolina (G.S. § 105-153.5(b)(5a)) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 12-6-1170/1171), where eligibility records and worksheets legally distinguish between a retiree's own service record and a surviving spouse's SBP annuity.

4. **Fix Senior Pension Source Lists in CO and GA**:
   * Add `military_retirement_pay` to `gov.states.co.tax.income.subtractions.pension.income_sources`.
   * Add `military_retirement_pay` to `gov.states.ga.tax.income.agi.exclusions.retirement.sources`.

5. **Fix Typo in Nebraska**:
   * Rename `ne_military_retirement_substraction.py` to `ne_military_retirement_subtraction.py`.

---

### 5. Verification Plan
- Add federal YAML test cases showing `military_retirement_pay` and `military_retirement_pay_survivors` increasing federal gross income, AGI, and income tax.
- Add California YAML test cases showing military retirement pay is properly subject to California income tax.
- Add multi-income state test cases (wages + military retirement pay) verifying that exempting military pay does not shelter wages.

items.title: Implement Vermont Seasonal Fuel Assistance regular heating assistance
items.body:
## Summary

Implement Vermont's Seasonal Fuel Assistance Program regular heating benefit, the state's LIHEAP heating component, for the 2025-26 and 2026-27 heating seasons. The Department for Children and Families, Economic Services Division, runs it under 33 V.S.A. chapter 26, the Seasonal Fuel Assistance Rules 2900-2927 (adopted June 22, 2024) and the Fuel Procedures of July 1, 2025. The benefit is a heat cost percentage set by the percentage of poverty, times a standard heating cost, times the payment rate, adjusted for subsidized housing and heat in rent.

## Scope

Regular seasonal heating assistance only, as part of the all-state LIHEAP effort: household size, gross income, the income limit, the benefit tables, the payment rate and the housing adjustments. Crisis fuel assistance (rules 3100-3113), the Heat and Eat benefit (33 V.S.A. 2605(h)), weatherization, tank and furnace repair or replacement, and cooling are out of scope. Late-application reductions and the roomer benefit need inputs the model lacks.

## Key rules

- Income limit: the monthly amount in P-2913 (2025-26; $2,412 for one person) or on the DCF page (2026-27; $2,461), but never above exactly 185% of the guideline (33 V.S.A. 2604(a)) or the LIHEAP maximum, the greater of 150% of the guideline and 60% of state median income (rule 2913(b); 42 U.S.C. 8624(b)(2)(B)). The printed amounts are 185% of a whole-dollar monthly guideline rounded half up, which exceeds 185% for some sizes (two people in 2026: $3,262 against $3,260.63); the LIHEAP maximum binds from size 10.
- Household: people living together as one economic unit who buy heating fuel in common or pay for heat in rent (rule 2901(a)(6)), with at least one citizen, national or qualified immigrant. Size leaves out ineligible members, such as an undocumented immigrant, but their income counts (rules 2903, 2907, 2914(a)(1); P-2910).
- Heating cost and responsibility: the primary heating fuel must be listed in the standard heating cost tables (rules 2901(a)(14), 2916(b)): natural gas, propane, oil, kerosene, electricity, and firewood, pellets and coal, for multi-family homes and for single-family and mobile homes, by 1, 2, 3 or 4+ bedrooms ($923 to $4,552; unchanged for 2026-27).
- Countable income: gross income of all members from the 30 days before application, on 3SquaresVT rules, with no deductions (rules 2910-2911; P-2910). Earnings, public assistance (SSI, Reach Up, General Assistance), pensions and retirement benefits, Social Security, veterans', disability, workers' and unemployment benefits, rent, child support, alimony, interest, dividends and trusts count. Excluded: earnings of a student under 18 living with a parent, lump sums, tax credits, 3SquaresVT, energy assistance and HUD payments (rule 2912).
- Benefit computation (rules 2914-2915; 33 V.S.A. 2605): the P-2914A table of monthly dollar bands (no 2026-27 edition is published) gives the percentage of poverty, which sets a heat cost percentage from 90% (under 75%) down to 66% (145% to 154%), then 33%, 30% and 27% up to 185%. Benefit = percentage x heating cost x payment rate, rounded down. DCF sets the rate each season and does not publish it; 51%, inferred from the FFY2026 plan's $2,089 maximum (floor(4,552 x 0.90 x 0.51)), is an estimate, reused for 2026-27 until DCF publishes a rate.
- Special housing (rule 2914(c); 33 V.S.A. 2605(e)-(f)): 100% when paying a fuel supplier outside Section 8 or other public housing; 55% in Section 8 or public housing; 30% with a $50 minimum when heat is in an unsubsidized rent; a $21 nominal benefit when heat is in a subsidized rent.

## Sources

- 33 V.S.A. § 2605: https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/section/33/026/02605

items.title: Implement New Mexico LIHEAP regular heating assistance
items.body:
## Summary

Implement New Mexico's LIHEAP regular heating benefit for FFY2026 and FFY2027. The Health Care Authority (HCA), Income Support Division, runs the program under 8.150 NMAC, effective July 1, 2024. Each eligible household receives one benefit per federal fiscal year (October 1 to September 30): its points times a point value set each year, $35 in FFY2026 and $40 in FFY2027.

## Scope

Regular heating assistance only, as part of the all-state LIHEAP effort: residence, citizenship and household size, countable gross income, the 150% income limit, heating responsibility (heat in rent, subsidized housing, gathered wood), and the point system (energy burden with the energy standard allowance, propane, income and vulnerable-member points). Crisis and life-threatening crisis intervention, households with only a cooling cost, supplemental benefits at the secretary's direction, tribal LIHEAP, weatherization and heating-equipment repair are out of scope.

## Key rules

- Income limit: gross income at or below 150% of the federal poverty guideline (8.150.100.9 D; plan section 2.1). FFY2026 uses the 2025 guideline and FFY2027 the 2026 guideline. The guides print monthly limits rounded to the nearest dollar: $1,956 for one person in FFY2026 and $1,995 in FFY2027. There is no categorical eligibility and no asset test (8.150.100.9 C; 8.150.510.8).
- Household: individuals living together who incur a heating or cooling cost, with at least one U.S. citizen or TANF-qualified noncitizen (8.150.410.8, .13). Members without a Social Security number or proof of application are not in the benefit group (8.150.410.15). An ineligible noncitizen's gross income is divided by all members and counted for the eligible members only (8.150.520.10).
- Heating cost and responsibility: the household must incur an energy cost, directly or through non-subsidized rent; households that gather their own wood qualify (8.150.410.9).
- Countable income: gross income of the 30 days before the determination (8.150.520.12 C). Earned income counts for members over the age of 18 and unearned income for all members (8.150.520.12 B). Self-employment counts at its net (8.150.520.9 C). Unearned income includes Social Security before the Medicare premium, SSI, retirement payments, unemployment, child support, TANF, interest, dividends and contributions from family or friends; lump sums, loans, the EITC and SNAP are excluded (8.150.520.8 B, .13). Where the plan's section 1.9 checklist differs (Medicare, lump sums, cash gifts, age 18), the rule governs.
- Benefit computation (8.150.620.9 and .10): energy burden points from the monthly heating bill over monthly income, with the bill raised to the energy standard allowance ($291 in FFY2026, $298 in FFY2027) when lower: 0 below 6%, 1 from 6%, 2 from 11%, 3 from 16%; plus 2 points for propane. Income points: 3 at or below 110% of the guideline, 2 above it. The rule says 100%; HCA's guides and the FFY2026 ISD 017 card use 110%, which the implementation follows and lists in `source_conflicts/candidates.yaml` (`us-nm:liheap-three-income-points`). Vulnerable points: 2 each for a member aged 5 or younger, 60 or older, or disabled, once per group. Benefit = points x point value: 2 to 14 points, $70 to $490 in FFY2026 and $80 to $560 in FFY2027.
- Special housing: heat included in non-subsidized rent qualifies, even with no designated cost. Subsidized tenants qualify only with a separate or additional out-of-pocket heating cost (8.150.410.11). Households with heat in rent, and households heating with wood they do not buy, receive no energy burden points (8.150.620.9 A(3)).

## Sources

- 8.150.110 NMAC, application process: https://www.srca.nm.gov/parts/title08/08.150.0110.html

items.title: Model Rhode Island Ticket to Work and Sherlock as separate Medicaid buy-in pathways
items.body:
Follow-up to #8493 and narrower successor to closed #8481. Rhode Island should be modeled separately, or at least as named subpathways behind the shared working-disabled buy-in category, because the current program is not one flat buy-in rule.

## Why this is separate from the shared schema

Rhode Island's current public EOHHS materials split Medicaid Programs for Working People with Disabilities into two named pathways:

- Ticket to Work (TTW), ages 16-64.
- Sherlock Plan, age 65 and older.

Those two pathways have different financial limits and premium schedules:

- TTW has no income limit and no asset limit.
- Sherlock has a 250% FPL income limit and a $10,000 individual / $20,000 couple asset limit.
- TTW premiums continue well above 250% FPL.
- Sherlock premiums only apply across the lower schedule up to its 250% FPL income limit.
- EOHHS says Sherlock participants as of September 2024 were automatically transitioned into TTW, and people in TTW nearing age 65 are evaluated for Sherlock after turning 65.

That is more than ordinary parameter variation. A single `age/min`, `age/max`, `income_limit`, and `asset_limit` row cannot represent both pathways without either losing the TTW no-limit rule or losing the Sherlock age-65+ rule.

## Source details

Rhode Island EOHHS page, last updated April 28, 2026:

- Programs for working people with disabilities are:
  - Ticket to Work, ages 16-64.
  - Sherlock Plan, ages 65+.
- Both provide full Medicaid medical benefits, HCBS/LTSS where applicable, and services needed to start or continue employment.
- TTW eligibility:
  - age 16-64 inclusive;
  - meet Medicaid disability requirements;
  - disability does not require inability to work;
  - proof of active paid employment;
  - no income limit;
  - no asset limit;
  - premiums based on FPL.
- TTW premium schedule:
  - 0 to <150% FPL: no premium;
  - 150 to <185% FPL: $61;
  - 185 to <200% FPL: $77;
  - 200 to <250% FPL: $92;
  - then increasing brackets through 900%+ FPL, with $370 at 900%+ FPL.
- Sherlock eligibility:
  - age 65 or older;
  - meet Medicaid disability requirements;
  - proof of active paid employment;
  - countable earned net income no greater than 250% FPL after SSI-related disregards;
  - countable assets no greater than $10,000 individual / $20,000 couple;
  - medical savings accounts, retirement accounts, and approved work-related items are excluded.
- Sherlock premium schedule:
  - 0 to <150% FPL: no premium;
  - 150 to <185% FPL: $61;
  - 185 to <200% FPL: $77;
  - 200 to <250% FPL: $92.

Rhode Island's administrative rule also describes the Sherlock Plan as an SSI-related eligibility pathway for working adults with disabilities and distinguishes non-LTSS coverage from LTSS coverage. That adds another reason to avoid flattening the Rhode Island rules into one generic row before checking how to handle LTSS and cost sharing.

## Implementation notes

- Create Rhode Island-specific variables or subpathway parameters for TTW and Sherlock rather than one state row.
- Feed both subpathways into the shared `WORKING_DISABLED_BUY_IN` category from #8493.
- Represent TTW no-income/no-asset limits explicitly instead of treating missing limits as unavailable coverage.
- Represent Sherlock income and asset limits separately from TTW.
- Add a premium table that can support TTW's extended brackets above 250% FPL.
- Verify whether LTSS Sherlock cost-sharing should be modeled in this issue or deferred to a separate LTSS/cost-sharing issue.
- Note the apparent source/version issue: the current EOHHS consumer page presents TTW as 16-64 and Sherlock as 65+, while older regulatory language describes Sherlock more broadly. The implementation should rely on current controlling authority and document the date/source used.

## Acceptance criteria

- A disabled Rhode Island worker age 16-64 with paid employment qualifies through TTW even when income/assets exceed the Sherlock limits.
- A disabled Rhode Island worker age 65+ with paid employment qualifies through Sherlock only if they meet the Sherlock income and asset tests.
- TTW and Sherlock both map to the shared working-disabled buy-in Medicaid category.
- TTW premiums are computed beyond 250% FPL using the Rhode Island schedule.
- Sherlock premiums stop at the schedule relevant to its 250% FPL income limit.
- Tests cover a 64-year-old TTW case, a 65-year-old Sherlock case, and a high-income TTW case with a premium above the Sherlock maximum.

## Sources

- Rhode Island EOHHS, Medicaid Programs For Working People With Disabilities: https://eohhs.ri.gov/Consumer/TheSherlockPlan.aspx
- Stay Covered Rhode Island, Adults With Disabilities: https://staycovered.ri.gov/your-medicaid-benefits/programs-services/adults-disabilities
- Rhode Island Department of State, 210-RICR-40-15-1, Medicaid for Working People with Disabilities Program: https://rules.sos.ri.gov/Regulations/part/210-40-15-1?reg_id=10076
- Sherlock Center on Disabilities, New expansion to Medicaid buy-in removes limits for workers with disabilities: https://sherlockcenter.ric.edu/news-stories/new-expansion-medicaid-buy-removes-limits-workers-disabilities

Related: #8493, #8481, #8102, #8497.
