items.title: is_usda_disabled: 7 CFR 271.2 requires benefit receipt; definition-only flag used and blind SSI recipients dropped
items.body:
Part of #9330 (disconnected disability inputs audit).

## Summary

`is_usda_disabled` — the flag behind SNAP's "elderly or disabled member" preferences (uncapped shelter deduction, medical expense deduction, no gross income test, relaxed asset test) — is built from the SSI disability *definition* flag, but 7 CFR 271.2 keys on *receipt* of benefits, with blindness payments on equal footing with disability payments. This is wrong in both directions.

## Current code

`policyengine_us/parameters/gov/usda/disabled_programs.yaml`:

```yaml
values:
  2021-01-01:
    - is_ssi_disabled
    - social_security_disability
    - is_permanently_disabled_veteran
    - is_surviving_spouse_of_disabled_veteran
    - is_surviving_child_of_disabled_veteran
```

consumed by `policyengine_us/variables/gov/usda/is_usda_disabled.py` via `np.logical_or.reduce`.

## Legal basis

[7 CFR 271.2](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/7/271.2), "Elderly or disabled member", item (2): a member who "**Receives** supplemental security income benefits under title XVI of the Social Security Act or disability or **blindness** payments under titles I, II, X, XIV, or XVI".

## Defects

1. **Under-inclusion (blind SSI recipients)**: a blind SSI recipient under 60 (`is_blind & ssi > 0`) typically has `meets_ssi_disability_criteria = False` (disconnected inputs), so `is_ssi_disabled = False` and nothing else in the list fires. Legally an elderly/disabled member; the model denies the uncapped shelter deduction (`snap_excess_shelter_expense_deduction.py:34`), applies the gross income test (`meets_snap_gross_income_test.py:30`) and standard asset limit (`meets_snap_asset_test.py:28`), and denies the medical expense deduction (`snap_excess_medical_expense_deduction.py:23`).
2. **Over-inclusion (definition without receipt)**: `is_ssi_disabled` has no income/resource/receipt test. Someone meeting §1614(a)(3) whose income is far above SSI limits and who receives no SSDI receives no benefit listed in 271.2 — legally NOT an elderly/disabled member — yet gets all four preferences.

## Proposed fix

Replace `is_ssi_disabled` with `ssi` in `disabled_programs.yaml` (receipt semantics; covers the blind and disabled bases at once; `logical_or.reduce` already handles dollar-valued entries like `social_security_disability`, so a dollar `ssi` entry works identically). Consider also `receives_ssi` for survey-reported receipt.

**Deliberate call needed**: `ssi > 0` embeds SSI takeup, so SNAP generosity would co-move with the takeup assignment in microsim; `uncapped_ssi > 0` is the takeup-neutral middle ground but weaker on the literal "receives" text.

## Related 271.2 coverage gaps (documentation, not code)

- State SSP receipt (271.2 items 3–4): largely subsumed by a receipt-based fix since nearly all state supplement variables gate on `ssi > 0`.
- Disability-based Medicaid with SSI-comparable criteria: partially representable via `medicaid_category`.
- Government disability retirement and Railroad Retirement disability annuities: **not representable** (no disability split in `railroad_benefits`); record as known non-modeling.

items.title: Model New Hampshire MEAD and MOAD as separate Medicaid buy-in pathways
items.body:
Follow-up to #8493 and narrower successor to closed #8472. New Hampshire should be modeled as separate named subpathways, or at least a state-specific overlay, because the state has both MEAD and MOAD with different age ranges, legal authorities, income logic, resource treatment, and premium rules.

## Why this is separate from the shared schema

The shared #8493 schema is a good fit for states where the rule is a single disabled-worker buy-in with one age band, one income limit, one asset limit, and maybe one premium formula. New Hampshire is not that simple:

- MEAD is Medicaid for Employed Adults with Disabilities, for ages 18-64.
- MOAD is Medicaid for Employed Older Adults with Disabilities, for age 65+.
- MEAD uses a 450% FPL net-income standard after APTD/ANB treatment and disregards.
- MOAD is authorized separately for older adults; the statute states 250% FPL, while the DHHS fact sheet says a special MOAD disregard makes the effective limit 450% FPG to align with MEAD.
- MEAD resources are based on a 2002 $20,000 individual / $30,000 couple limit updated annually by CPI, not a fixed simple limit.
- Resource exclusions include retirement plans, medical savings accounts, and employability accounts for work-related goods and services.
- MEAD has a premium as a condition of eligibility, with a tiered 7.5% FPL-based structure and a separate full-premium rule when annual AGI exceeds $75,000.
- Employment requires paid work with FICA contributions, or self-employment with SECA documentation.
- MEAD has temporary unemployment continuation rules.

Those differences justify modeling MEAD/MOAD explicitly. A single state row risks mixing adult and older-adult pathways, under-modeling the income disregard, and missing the premium condition.

## Source details

New Hampshire Admin. Code He-W 841.03 for MEAD:

- MEAD applies to applicants age 18 through 64.
- Applicants must meet APTD or ANB general and technical requirements.
- Applicants must meet MEAD medical criteria.
- Applicants must be employed for pay or self-employed for pay at application, during eligibility determination, and during any retroactive coverage period.
- Net income is determined using APTD or ANB treatment and disregards, including spouse income if applicable, and must not exceed 450% of federal poverty guidelines.
- Countable resources must not exceed the 2002 limit of $20,000 individual / $30,000 married couple, updated annually by CPI.
- Employment for pay requires remuneration and FICA contributions.
- Self-employment requires SECA payment documentation.
- Excluded resources include retirement plans, medical savings accounts, and MEAD employability accounts.
- Employability accounts can cover work-related goods and services such as business equipment, training, work-related attendant care, medical devices, tools, transportation, vehicle purchases or modifications, and disability-related medical supplies.
- A MEAD recipient who becomes unemployed but intends to return to work can remain eligible for a 6-month extension in specified circumstances, with one possible additional 6-month extension.
- Cost-free employer or organization health insurance must be used to remain eligible.

New Hampshire RSA 167:3-m for MOAD:

- MOAD is a Medicaid work incentive program for employed older adults with disabilities.
- It is intended to support workers age 65 and older with disabilities.
- It excludes resources accumulated from earnings in a separate account when determining future eligibility for other medical assistance programs.
- It provides continued eligibility during temporary unemployment in specified circumstances.
- It permits self-employment below the federal minimum wage.
- It permits HCBS waiver-eligible people who meet a special income limit to receive assistance through MOAD.
- The statute states MOAD eligibility where income does not exceed 250% FPL and SSI criteria are met.

New Hampshire premium rule He-C 5003.01 for MEAD:

- MEAD recipients must pay a monthly premium as a condition of eligibility.
- Premiums cannot exceed 7.5% of net income for recipients with combined net income at or below 450% FPL.
- No premium below 150% FPL.
- Premiums are tiered based on 150%, 200%, 250%, 300%, 350%, and 400% FPL thresholds.
- If annual adjusted gross income exceeds $75,000, the full premium is 7.5% of AGI.
- Nonpayment for 2 consecutive months without good cause terminates MEAD.

The 2024 DHHS fact sheet summarizes MEAD and MOAD together:

- MEAD is for ages 18-64; MOAD is for ages 65+.
- People must be employed or self-employed for pay, contribute to FICA, meet income/resource criteria, meet ANB/APTD medical criteria or have a listed impairment expected to last 48 months or longer, and enroll in cost-free employer health insurance if offered.
- The fact sheet notes the MOAD net income limit is below 250% FPG, but a special MOAD disregard makes the effective limit 450% FPG, aligning it with MEAD.

## Implementation notes

- Add New Hampshire-specific MEAD and MOAD variables or a subpathway dimension under the shared buy-in category.
- Feed qualifying MEAD and MOAD cases into the shared `WORKING_DISABLED_BUY_IN` Medicaid category from #8493.
- Model age bands separately:
  - MEAD: 18-64;
  - MOAD: 65+.
- Model MEAD income using net income after APTD/ANB treatment and disregards, not gross MAGI.
- Decide how to represent MOAD's statutory 250% FPL rule and the effective 450% FPG limit from the special disregard.
- Parameterize CPI-updated resource limits, or set annual values from a current state source if CPI reconstruction is too much for the first pass.
- Defer detailed employability-account asset treatment if needed, but document the approximation.
- Decide whether MEAD premiums are implemented in this issue or a linked premium issue, but do not ignore them in eligibility because payment is a condition of eligibility.

## Acceptance criteria

- A New Hampshire disabled worker age 18-64 who meets MEAD employment, income, and resource rules qualifies through MEAD.
- A New Hampshire disabled worker age 65+ is evaluated under MOAD rather than MEAD.
- MEAD and MOAD both map to the shared `WORKING_DISABLED_BUY_IN` Medicaid category.
- Tests cover:
  - MEAD age boundary at 18 and 65;
  - MOAD age 65+;
  - income above ordinary ABD limits but within MEAD/MOAD buy-in limits;
  - resource treatment above ordinary ABD limits but within the buy-in limits;
  - a MEAD premium case above 150% FPL if premiums are included in the PR.
- Source comments explain the 250% statutory MOAD limit vs the effective 450% FPG note from the DHHS fact sheet.

## Sources

- N.H. Admin. Code He-W 841.03, Medicaid for Employed Adults with Disabilities (MEAD): https://regulations.justia.com/states/new-hampshire/he/subtitle-he-w/chapter-he-w-800/part-he-w-841/section-he-w-841-03/
- N.H. Rev. Stat. 167:3-m, MOAD Work Incentive Program: https://law.justia.com/codes/new-hampshire/title-xii/chapter-167/section-167-3-m/
- N.H. Admin. Code He-C 5003.01, Premium Schedule for MEAD: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-hampshire/N-H-Admin-Code-SS-He-C-5003.01
- New Hampshire DHHS Program Fact Sheet 2024: https://nhlwaa.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/DHHS-Program-Fact-Sheet-2024.pdf

Related: #8493, #8472, #8102, #8497.

items.title: MA Senior Circuit Breaker adds in-kind SNAP and WIC to total income, contrary to M.G.L. c.62 § 6(k)(1)
items.body:
## Summary

`ma_scb_total_income` adds SNAP and WIC back into total income for the Massachusetts Senior Circuit Breaker credit. M.G.L. c.62 § 6(k)(1) adds back cash public assistance but explicitly excludes in-kind assistance, so neither belongs in the add-back list.

## Statutory text

M.G.L. c.62 § 6(k)(1) defines "taxpayer's total income" as the sum of Part A, B, and C adjusted gross income, increased by, to the extent excluded or subtracted from AGI:

> "the total amount of income and receipts from social security, retirement, pension, or annuities, **cash, but not in-kind, public assistance**, tax-exempt interest and dividends, net capital losses deducted pursuant to paragraph (2) of subsection (c) of section 2, net losses in any class of Part C adjusted gross income as defined in subsection (e) of section 2, capital gains deducted pursuant to subparagraph (K) of paragraph (1) of subsection (d) of section 2, income from a partnership or trust not included therein and gross receipts from any other source other than assistance received by this subsection"

SNAP and WIC are in-kind nutrition assistance, so the "but not in-kind" clause excludes them.

Source: https://malegislature.gov/Laws/GeneralLaws/PartI/TitleIX/Chapter62/Section6

## Current encoding

`policyengine_us/parameters/gov/states/ma/tax/income/credits/senior_circuit_breaker/income/disallowed_deductions.yaml`

```yaml
values:
  2001-01-01:
    - social_security
    - tax_exempt_unemployment_compensation
    - tax_exempt_pension_income
    - tax_exempt_interest_income
    - snap        # line 8  — in-kind, should not be added back
    - ssi
    - ma_state_supplement
    - tanf
    - wic         # line 12 — in-kind, should not be added back
```

The remaining entries are correct: `ssi`, `tanf`, and `ma_state_supplement` are cash public assistance, and `social_security` and the three `tax_exempt_*` items are named explicitly in the statute.

## Impact

`ma_scb_total_income` returns `max_(0, ma_gross_income + disallowed_deductions - exemptions)`, and `ma_senior_circuit_breaker` uses that income in two places:

1. `income_threshold = income * scb.amount.min_real_estate_tax` — the property-tax floor the credit phases in above. Overstated income raises the floor and shrinks `ret_over_threshold`.
2. `meets_max_income_condition = income <= scb.eligibility.max_income[filing_status]` — a hard cliff. Overstated income can push a household over it and zero the credit.

Both effects run the same direction: the model **understates** the credit for SNAP and WIC recipients age 65+. The credit is refundable (`gov/states/ma/tax/income/credits/refundable.yaml`), so the error flows through to `household_net_income`.

## Fix

Remove `snap` and `wic` from the list. No formula change.

## Tasks

- [ ] Remove the two entries
- [ ] Add a test asserting SNAP and WIC do not raise `ma_scb_total_income`, and one asserting cash assistance still does
- [ ] Confirm no partner contract test covers MA SCB (none found)

items.title: NE Child Care Subsidy uses federal AGI for eligibility and SPM net income for the family fee instead of gross countable income per 392 NAC 2-010
items.body:
## Current behavior

The Nebraska Child Care Subsidy model uses two different income measures, neither of which matches the program's legal income definition:

**Eligibility** (`ne_child_care_subsidy_income_eligible`) sums federal adjusted gross income across the SPM unit:

```python
income = add(spm_unit, period, ["adjusted_gross_income"])
fpg = spm_unit("spm_unit_fpg", period)
income_limit = fpg * p.initial_eligibility
return income <= income_limit
```

**Family fee** (`ne_child_care_subsidy`) uses SPM unit net income:

```python
income = spm_unit("spm_unit_net_income", period)
...
capped_childcare_expenses_with_fee = max_(childcare_expenses - p.rate * income, 0)
```

`spm_unit_net_income` adds `spm_unit_benefits` (SNAP, TANF, housing subsidies, energy assistance, etc.) and subtracts taxes and SPM expenses.

## Legal income definition

[Neb. Rev. Stat. §68-1206](https://nebraskalegislature.gov/laws/statutes.php?statute=68-1206) sets eligibility in terms of **gross income**: initial eligibility up to 185% of the federal poverty level (subsection (2)(a)), transitional child care while income stays at or below 200% FPL, or through the certification period while under 85% of state median income (subsection (2)(b)(i)), and a disregard of 10% of a household's gross earned income after twelve continuous months on the program.

The detailed countable-income rules are in 392 NAC 2-010, restated in DHHS's current [Title 392 guidance document](https://dhhs.ne.gov/Guidance%20Docs/Title%20392%20-%20Child%20Care%20Subsidy.pdf#page=3) (income sources on page 3, the 7%-of-gross-income sliding fee under 2-011 on page 4, and the 185%/200%/85% SMI tiers on page 5). The [compiled Title 392 regulations](https://dhhs.ne.gov/Documents/Title-392-Complete.pdf#page=13) list the same 28 countable sources (page 13) and the income exclusions (page 15).

**Countable sources** (392 NAC 2-010.01(A), items 1–28) include: **SSI**; **AABD payments**; gross wages/salary before any deductions (including armed forces pay, tips, commissions, bonuses); in-kind income received in lieu of wages; RSDI and Railroad Retirement **before Medicare premium deductions**; dividends and interest; rental and land-lease income; net royalties; retirement pensions; veterans' pensions; military allotments; contributions; lump sums (prorated over six months); annuities; unemployment compensation; workers' compensation; **court-ordered child, spousal, and cash medical support**; payments by an absent parent to the client for child care, rent, or house payments; and net self-employment income.

**Self-employment** (392 NAC 3-005.02B): gross self-employment income (including capital gains) minus a standard 49% disregard when at least one allowable expense is reported; income tax returns can document actual expenses instead.

**Excluded** (392 NAC 3-005.03): the ADC (TANF) grant; EITC payments; tax refunds; gifts; loans; lump-sum inheritances or insurance payments; **capital gains** (outside self-employment); SNAP and other federal nutrition benefits; **earnings of a child age 18 or younger who is in school**; educational grants; adoption or guardianship subsidies; LIHEAP; HUD or local housing assistance; disaster assistance; work-expense reimbursements; and military combat pay.

## Discrepancies

Eligibility side (federal AGI vs. gross countable income):

| Income type | Legal rule | Federal AGI |
|---|---|---|
| SSI | Counted (item 1) | Absent |
| AABD payment | Counted (item 2) — the model computes `ne_aabd` | Absent |
| Child support received | Counted (item 25) | Absent |
| Workers' compensation | Counted (item 24) | Absent |
| Veterans' pensions | Counted (item 17) | Absent |
| Social Security (RSDI) | Counted gross, before Medicare premiums (item 7) | Only the taxable portion (0–85%) |
| Wages | Gross, before pre-tax deductions | After above-the-line deductions (IRA, student loan interest, ½ SE tax, etc.) |
| Capital gains | Excluded outside self-employment | Included |
| Earnings of a child ≤18 in school | Excluded | Included when the child files (AGI is summed across the unit's tax units) |
| Self-employment | Gross minus 49% standard disregard | Net profit minus ½ SE tax deduction |

Fee side (`spm_unit_net_income` vs. gross income): the 7% family fee legally applies to the household's **gross income** (2-011 guidance), but the model applies it to net income, which counts legally excluded benefits (TANF grant, SNAP, LIHEAP, housing subsidies) and subtracts taxes and SPM expenses. `ne_child_care_subsidies` is not part of `spm_unit_benefits`, so there is no circularity today — this is purely a definitional mismatch.

## Related gaps (not modeled at the moment)

- The 10% gross earned income disregard after 12 continuous months (§68-1206(2)(b)(i)).
- Transitional Child Care: ongoing eligibility up to 200% FPL / 85% SMI; the model applies only the initial 185% FPL test.

## Suggested fix

Create a `ne_child_care_subsidy_countable_income` variable built from parameter-listed sources (employment income, self-employment income, SSI, `ne_aabd`, Social Security, pensions, unemployment compensation, workers' compensation, child support received, etc.), with a person-level mask exempting the earned income of children in school, and use it in both `ne_child_care_subsidy_income_eligible` and the family-fee calculation in `ne_child_care_subsidy`.

items.title: Enforce 401(k) and 403(b) elective deferral limits (IRC §402(g))
items.body:
## Current behavior

The variables [`traditional_401k_contributions`](policyengine_us/variables/household/expense/retirement/traditional_401k_contributions.py), [`roth_401k_contributions`](policyengine_us/variables/household/expense/retirement/roth_401k_contributions.py), [`traditional_403b_contributions`](policyengine_us/variables/household/expense/retirement/traditional_403b_contributions.py), and [`roth_403b_contributions`](policyengine_us/variables/household/expense/retirement/roth_403b_contributions.py) are all pure input variables (no formula). Whatever value comes in from microdata or user input flows through unmodified to:

- `pre_tax_contributions` (reducing `irs_employment_income` for the traditional variants)
- `savers_credit_qualified_contributions`
- Various state retirement adjustments

The IRC §402(g) elective deferral limit ($23,000 in 2024, $23,500 in 2025, $24,500 in 2026) is **defined as a parameter** but **never enforced** as a cap on the contribution amounts.

## Gap

- Parameter [`gov.irs.gross_income.retirement_contributions.limit.401k`](policyengine_us/parameters/gov/irs/gross_income/retirement_contributions/limit/401k.yaml) is defined with correct values and uprating, but no variable applies it.
- The catch-up parameter [`gov.irs.gross_income.retirement_contributions.catch_up.limit.k401`](policyengine_us/parameters/gov/irs/gross_income/retirement_contributions/catch_up/limit/k401.yaml) is age-bracketed (including the SECURE 2.0 super catch-up for ages 60-63) and computed in `k401_catch_up_limit.py`, but is not applied to actual contributions either.
- Households in survey microdata could have contributions exceeding the statutory limit, and reforms simulating elective-deferral cap changes have no effect because the cap is not modeled in the baseline.

Note: §402(g) limits the **combined** total of elective deferrals across all 401(k) and 403(b) plans (traditional + Roth), so the cap should be applied to the sum, not to each variable individually.

## Proposed fix

Apply the existing PolicyEngine \"reported vs. actual\" pattern (see e.g., `ssi_reported`, `medicare_part_b_premiums_reported`):

1. Add input variables holding raw/survey-reported amounts:
   - `traditional_401k_contributions_reported`
   - `roth_401k_contributions_reported`
   - `traditional_403b_contributions_reported`
   - `roth_403b_contributions_reported`

2. Make the existing variables formulas that apply the combined §402(g) cap:

   ```python
   limit = base_402g_limit + catch_up_if_eligible  # uses k401_catch_up_limit (handles age 60-63 super catch-up)
   total_reported = sum of all reported variants
   scale = where(total_reported > limit, limit / max(total_reported, 1), 1)
   actual = reported * scale
   ```

   Proportional scaling preserves the relative mix of traditional vs. Roth and 401(k) vs. 403(b) when the combined total exceeds the cap.

3. Move uprating of contribution amounts from the formula variables to the `_reported` inputs in [`policyengine_us/tools/default_uprating.py`](policyengine_us/tools/default_uprating.py).

## Files affected

- New: `policyengine_us/variables/household/expense/retirement/{traditional,roth}_{401k,403b}_contributions_reported.py`
- New: shared `elective_deferral_limit.py` variable (base + catch-up)
- Modified: existing 401(k)/403(b) contribution variable files (becomes formulas)
- Modified: `policyengine_us/tools/default_uprating.py`
- New: YAML test under `policyengine_us/tests/policy/baseline/household/expense/retirement/`

## Backwards compatibility

`traditional_401k_contributions` etc. remain valid output variable names — they are now derived rather than inputs. Tests and downstream code that *consume* these values are unaffected. API callers that *set* them as input must switch to the `_reported` suffix.

## Statutory references

- [26 USC §402(g)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/402#g) — elective deferral limit
- [26 USC §414(v)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/414#v) — catch-up contributions (including SECURE 2.0 enhanced catch-up for ages 60-63)
- IRS Notice 2024-80 ($23,500 limit for 2025)

items.title: Illinois Health Benefits for Workers with Disabilities (Medicaid buy-in)
items.body:
## Program Overview
Illinois Health Benefits for Workers with Disabilities (HBWD) is a Medicaid buy-in program administered by the Department of Healthcare and Family Services (HFS) that allows working individuals with disabilities ages 16-64 to maintain healthcare coverage while earning income. The program features higher asset limits ($25,000 vs standard Medicaid's $2,000) and charges income-based monthly premiums calculated from a 2D table.

**Legal Authority:** 89 Ill. Admin. Code § 120.510 (effective 2022-03-25)

---

## Eligibility Determination

**All criteria must be met:**

1. **Age:** Between 16 and 64 years old (bracket parameter with `p.age.calc(age)`)

2. **Disability:** Meets SSA disability definition OR receives Social Security disability benefits

3. **Employment:** Must have earned income (employment or self-employment)

4. **Income:** Household countable income ≤ 350% Federal Poverty Level
   - Individual + spouse income combined per § 120.510(f)
   - SPMUnit-level calculation

5. **Assets:** Household non-exempt assets ≤ $25,000
   - Cash assets + countable vehicle value
   - Vehicle exemption: Full if essential, $4,500 if not (§ 120.381)

6. **Immigration:** U.S. citizen or qualified noncitizen
   - Refugee, asylee, LPR, conditional entrant, paroled ≥1 year

---

## Income Calculation (SPMUnit Level)

### Step 1: Gross Earned Income
Sum across household members:
- Employment income
- Self-employment income

### Step 2: Apply Work Expense Deductions (§ 120.370)
Currently implemented:
- State withheld income tax
- Employee Social Security tax (FICA)
- Child care expenses ($128/month part-time, $160/month full-time ≥100 hours)

Not yet implemented (legally allowed):
- Transportation (19¢/mile), meals (15-45¢/day), uniforms, union dues
- Insurance premiums, retirement withholdings, disability work items

### Step 3: Apply Earned Income Exemptions (§ 120.362)
- **$25 flat exemption** (applied to unearned first, remainder to earned)
- **$20 + 50% of next $60** for disabled workers (total $50 exemption)
- Combined: **$75 total earned income exemption**

Uses `il_aabd_earned_income_after_exemption_person` (identical values in § 120.362 and § 113.120)

### Step 4: Gross Unearned Income
Sum across household members:
- Social Security (retirement, survivors, disability)
- Workers compensation, unemployment compensation
- Investment income (dividends, interest, capital gains)
- Alimony, farm income, retirement distributions, miscellaneous

**Excluded:** SSI is not counted for HBWD

### Step 5: Household Countable Income
```
Countable Income (SPMUnit) = 
    Sum(Earned after expenses & exemptions) + 
    Sum(Unearned income excluding SSI)
```

Compared against 350% FPL for household size

---

## Premium Calculation (Person Level)

**2-Array Additive Approach:**

Instead of storing a 441-cell 2D table, we discovered the premium table is **98.6% additive**:
- Premium ≈ Earned Component(countable earned) + Unearned Component(countable unearned)
- Capped at $500

**Implementation:**
```python
earned_component = p.earned_component.calc(earned)  # 21-bracket parameter
unearned_component = p.unearned_component.calc(unearned)  # 21-bracket parameter
premium = min_(earned_component + unearned_component, 500)
```

**Accuracy:** 435/441 cells exact match, 6 cells differ by $1

**Premium Brackets** (effective 2022-04-01, $250 increments):

| Income Range | Earned | Unearned | Income Range | Earned | Unearned |
|--------------|--------|----------|--------------|--------|----------|
| $0-250 | $0 | $0 | $2501-2750 | $63 | $188 |
| $251-500 | $6 | $19 | $2751-3000 | $69 | $206 |
| $501-750 | $13 | $38 | $3001-3250 | $75 | $225 |
| $751-1000 | $19 | $56 | $3251-3500 | $81 | $244 |
| $1001-1250 | $25 | $75 | $3501-3750 | $88 | $263 |
| $1251-1500 | $31 | $94 | $3751-4000 | $94 | $281 |
| $1501-1750 | $38 | $113 | $4001-4250 | $100 | $300 |
| $1751-2000 | $44 | $131 | $4251-4500 | $106 | $319 |
| $2001-2250 | $50 | $150 | $4501-4750 | $113 | $338 |
| $2251-2500 | $56 | $169 | $4751-5000 | $119 | $356 |
|              |        |          | $5000+ | $125 | $375 |

**Example:** Worker with $2,000 employment + $1,000 social_security
- Household earned after exemptions: ~$1,713
- Household unearned: $1,000  
- Individual premium: $38 (earned bracket 6) + $75 (unearned bracket 4) = **$113**

---

## Asset Calculation (Person Level)

**Countable Assets:**
```
Countable Assets (Person) = 
    SPM Unit Cash Assets + 
    SPM Unit Countable Vehicle Value
```

**Vehicle Exemption** (§ 120.381, identical to AABD § 113.141):
- **Full exemption** if vehicle is essential (employment, medical, handicapped, terrain)
- **$4,500 exemption** for one non-essential vehicle
- Uses `il_aabd_countable_vehicle_value` (same rules, same parameter)

**Not yet implemented:**
- Homestead (primary residence) exemption
- Retirement account exemptions  
- Burial fund exemptions
- Life insurance exemptions

---

## Implementation Structure

```
policyengine_us/
├── parameters/gov/states/il/hfs/hbwd/ (11 parameters)
│   ├── eligibility/
│   │   ├── age.yaml (bracket: 16-64)
│   │   ├── income_limit_fpg_percent.yaml (3.5 = 350%)
│   │   └── asset_limit.yaml ($25,000)
│   ├── income/sources/
│   │   ├── earned.yaml (employment_income, self_employment_income)
│   │   └── unearned.yaml (14 income types, excludes SSI)
│   ├── premium/
│   │   ├── earned_component.yaml (21 brackets)
│   │   └── unearned_component.yaml (21 brackets)
│   └── qualified_noncitizen_status.yaml (6 statuses)
│
├── variables/gov/states/il/hfs/hbwd/ (15 variables)
│   ├── eligibility/ (7 variables - all Person entity)
│   ├── income/
│   │   ├── earned/
│   │   │   ├── il_hbwd_gross_earned_income.py (Person, adds)
│   │   │   └── il_hbwd_countable_earned_income.py (Person, adds AABD exemption)
│   │   ├── unearned/
│   │   │   └── il_hbwd_countable_unearned_income.py (Person, adds)
│   │   └── il_hbwd_countable_income.py (SPMUnit, sums household)
│   ├── asset/
│   │   └── il_hbwd_countable_assets.py (Person, cash + vehicles)
│   ├── il_hbwd_premium.py (Person, 2-array lookup)
│   ├── il_hbwd_person.py (Person, negative premium)
│   └── il_hbwd.py (SPMUnit, aggregates)
│
└── tests/ (11 test files, 51 test cases)
    ├── eligibility/ (6 test files)
    ├── asset/ (1 test file)
    ├── il_hbwd_premium.yaml (6 tests)
    ├── il_hbwd_person.yaml (3 tests)
    └── integration.yaml (7 scenarios)
```

---

## Key Technical Decisions

**Reuse AABD Variables Where Rules Are Identical:**
- `il_aabd_earned_income_after_exemption_person` - § 120.362 and § 113.120 have same $75 exemption
- `il_aabd_countable_vehicle_value` - § 120.381 and § 113.141 have same $4,500 exemption
- Documented with comments explaining parallel legal authority

**Entity Levels:**
- Person: Eligibility components, individual income/premium
- SPMUnit: Household countable income (aggregates spouse income per § 120.510(f))
- SPMUnit: Final benefit aggregation

**Premium Innovation:**
- 2-array additive approach: 42 parameter values instead of 441
- 98.6% accuracy (only 6 cells differ by $1)
- Hardcoded $500 cap in formula (implicit from table maximum)

**Testing Strategy:**
- Only test variables with formulas (not `adds`-only variables)
- Use `absolute_error_margin: 0.01` for dollar amounts
- Stub intermediate values (Option C approach) for clean premium tests
- 7 integration scenarios with inline calculation comments

**Reference Standards:**
- All legal citations use law.cornell.edu format
- All parameters effective 2022-04-01 (regulation amendment date)
- All labels use "Illinois HBWD" abbreviation format
- Descriptions follow AABD/TANF patterns ("Illinois [verb]...")

items.body:
## Summary

Update the Arizona income tax model for tax year 2025. This includes updating parameter values, adding 2025 references to all parameters, and implementing new modelable programs.

This test fails because PEUS produces zero for `ri_income_tax` because it thinks the taxpayer is ineligible for the RI property tax credit.   Hand calculations using the 2021 form give the same results as TAXSIM35: a refundable RI property tax credit of $415.

items.title: Add 2021 Utah retirement credit and taxpayer credit parameters
items.body: The Utah state income tax code has several problems. The integration test presented below illustrates two of those problems. **First**, the taxpayer credit is incorrect because PolicyEngineUS projects the 2022 phase-out threshold value (which is correct) back to 2021. This is happening even though earlier in the development of the Utah income tax the 2021 parameter values were in the code. This can be seen in the following screenshot of a March 23rd code review session for pull request #1994. When #1994 was merged a month later, the 2021 values had been removed. This is just one example of the many missing 2021 parameter values. The 2021 parameter values are **missing** because some Utah tax parameters are specified as far back as 2020, 2018, and even 2008. **Second**, the retirement credit is incorrect. PolicyEngineUS generates a retirement credit for this test case that is zero when following the TC-40 form instructions produces a value of $624.50. The $624.50 retirement credit is also generated by TAXSIM35. Here is the integration test case followed by the test results: ``` - name: Tax unit with taxsimid 95281 in p21.its.csv and p21.ots.csv absolute_error_margin: 0.01 period: 2021 input: people: person1: is_tax_unit_head: true age: 73 employment_income: 21_010 ssi: 0 # not in TAXSIM35 state_supplement: 0 # not in TAXSIM35 wic: 0 # not in TAXSIM35 person2: is_tax_unit_spouse: true age: 73 employment_income: 22_010 ssi: 0 # not in TAXSIM35 state_supplement: 0 # not in TAXSIM35 wic: 0 # not in TAXSIM35 spm_units: spm_unit: members: [person1, person2] snap: 0 # not in TAXSIM35 tanf: 0 # not in TAXSIM35 tax_units: tax_unit: members: [person1, person2] premium_tax_credit: 0 # not in TAXSIM35 households: household: members: [person1, person2] state_code: UT output: # expected results from patched TAXSIM35 2023-04-24 version ut_income_tax: 3.78 ``` This test case produces these results: ``` Test 'Tax unit with taxsimid 95281 in p21.its.csv and p21.ots.csv': ut_income_tax@2021: [616.50195] differs from 3.7799999713897705 with an absolute margin [612.7219] > 0.01 ```
